Chapter overview

Tamil Nadu’s role in the freedom struggle developed from early regional resistance to political associations, nationalist journalism, Swadeshi, Home Rule, Gandhian mass movements, labour action, Quit India and INA participation.

Early resistanceAssociations & pressSwadeshi & Home RuleMass movementsQuit India & INA
Scope, Phases and Madras Presidency Context

The freedom struggle in Tamil Nadu moved from early armed resistance to associations, journalism, Swadeshi, Gandhian mass movements, Quit India and INA participation within the wider Madras Presidency context.

Scope of the Chapter

Tamil Nadu’s contribution to the Indian freedom struggle developed through several stages:

  • Early armed resistance against the East India Company
  • Formation of political associations
  • Growth of nationalist newspapers
  • Participation in the Indian National Congress
  • Swadeshi economic resistance
  • Revolutionary nationalism
  • Home Rule agitation
  • Gandhian mass movements
  • Labour and student participation
  • Civil Disobedience
  • Quit India
  • Indian National Army participation

The struggle was not restricted to a few prominent leaders. Merchants, lawyers, journalists, poets, workers, peasants, students, women and members of the Tamil diaspora participated in different phases.

Madras Presidency and Present-Day Tamil Nadu

During British rule, present-day Tamil Nadu formed part of the much larger Madras Presidency.

The Presidency also included substantial territories belonging to present-day:

  • Andhra Pradesh
  • Karnataka
  • Kerala
  • Odisha

Therefore, statistics relating to “Madras” or the “Madras Presidency” should not automatically be treated as figures relating only to present-day Tamil Nadu.

For example:

  • Delegates described as coming from Madras in early Congress sessions represented the larger Presidency.
  • Presidency-wide strikes and protests could have occurred outside the present boundaries of Tamil Nadu.
Broad Phases
Early Armed Resistance

Regional rulers and Palayakkarars opposed:

  • Company revenue demands
  • Loss of political authority
  • British territorial expansion
  • Interference in traditional administration
Constitutional Nationalism

Educated Indians formed associations and used:

  • Petitions
  • Resolutions
  • Public meetings
  • Newspapers
  • Legislative debate
  • Memoranda to the government
Mass Nationalism

From the Swadeshi period onward, nationalism increasingly involved:

  • Economic boycott
  • Swadeshi industries
  • Political speeches in Tamil
  • Labour strikes
  • Student participation
  • Satyagraha
  • Civil disobedience
  • Mass arrest
Sources

Important sources for studying the freedom struggle in Tamil Nadu include:

  • Company and colonial records
  • Government proceedings
  • Trial records
  • Police and prison reports
  • Congress resolutions
  • Newspapers and journals
  • Political speeches
  • Autobiographies
  • Personal correspondence
  • Songs and poems
  • Memorials
  • Oral traditions

Colonial records may describe anti-British leaders as rebels or criminals. Nationalist and oral traditions may sometimes exaggerate events. Both must be compared carefully.

Early Resistance: An Overview

Early resistance was regional and military; this topic gives only the chronology needed before the detailed treatment in Chapter 18.

Early resistance in Tamil Nadu preceded the emergence of organised nationalism and the Indian National Congress.

This topic provides only a chronological overview. Detailed accounts of the leaders, wars, proclamations, forts and executions belong to Chapter 18 — Early Agitations Against British Rule.

Puli Thevar
  • Puli Thevar was the Palayakkarar of Nerkattumseval.
  • His principal resistance lasted from 1755 to 1767.
  • He opposed the revenue authority of the Nawab of Arcot and the East India Company.
  • He organised a confederacy of western Palayakkarars.
  • He attempted to obtain support from Hyder Ali and the French.
  • He was defeated in 1767.
Velu Nachiyar
  • Velu Nachiyar was the queen of Sivaganga.
  • Her husband Muthu Vaduganatha Thevar was killed at Kalaiyar Kovil in 1772.
  • She took refuge at Virupachi.
  • She obtained support from Gopala Nayak and Hyder Ali.
  • She later recovered Sivaganga with the assistance of the Marudhu Brothers.
  • Kuyili is remembered in tradition as a commander in her forces.

Detailed information about Velu Nachiyar and Kuyili belongs mainly to Chapters 18 and 19.

Veerapandiya Kattabomman
  • Kattabomman was the Palayakkarar of Panchalankurichi.
  • His dispute with the Company centred on tribute, revenue collection and political interference.
  • The Company captured Panchalankurichi in 1799.
  • Kattabomman was executed at Kayathar on 16 October 1799.
  • His brother Oomathurai later joined the Marudhu-led resistance.
Marudhu Brothers
  • Periya Marudhu and Chinna Marudhu led resistance from Sivaganga.
  • The uprising of 1800–1801 is called the South Indian Rebellion or Second Palayakkarar War.
  • They issued the Tiruchirappalli Proclamation in June 1801.
  • It appealed for unity across region, caste, creed and religion against British authority.
  • The Marudhu Brothers were executed at Tiruppattur on 24 October 1801.
Dheeran Chinnamalai
  • Dheeran Chinnamalai’s original name was Theerthagiri.
  • He organised resistance in the Kongu region.
  • Odanilai became an important centre of his activities.
  • He adopted guerrilla methods.
  • He was executed at Sankagiri Fort on 31 July 1805.
Vellore Revolt
  • The Vellore Revolt broke out on 10 July 1806.
  • It was an uprising by Indian soldiers stationed at Vellore Fort.
  • Military dress regulations and interference with religious and social customs were immediate causes.
  • Members of Tipu Sultan’s family were confined in the fort.
  • The revolt was suppressed by forces led by Colonel Gillespie.
  • It preceded the Revolt of 1857 by more than fifty years.

Early resistance was mainly regional and military. The later nationalist movement created province-wide and all-India political organisations.

Political Associations and the Rise of Nationalism

The Madras Native Association and Madras Mahajana Sabha created the institutional base for organised political nationalism in the Presidency.

By the middle of the nineteenth century, an educated middle class emerged in Madras and began taking an interest in public affairs.

Political associations created an institutional foundation for organised nationalism.

Madras Native Association

The Madras Native Association was founded in 1852.

Important personalities included:

  • Gazulu Lakshminarasu Chetty
  • Srinivasanar
  • Their associates

Important features:

  • It was one of the earliest public political organisations in South India.
  • Its membership consisted largely of merchants.
  • It demanded reduction of taxation.
  • It opposed government support for missionary activity.
  • It drew attention to the condition of cultivators.
  • It exposed the use of torture by revenue officials.
  • Its representations contributed to an official investigation known as the Torture Commission.
  • The association had ceased to function by 1862.

The organisation was not yet a mass nationalist movement. It mainly represented public grievances through petitions and representations.

Madras Mahajana Sabha

The Madras Mahajana Sabha was founded on 16 May 1884.

Its founders included:

  • M. Veeraraghavachariar
  • P. Anandacharlu
  • P. Rangaiah Naidu
  • Other public figures

Important office-bearers:

  • First president — P. Rangaiah Naidu
  • Secretary — P. Anandacharlu
Major Demands

The Sabha demanded:

  • Simultaneous Civil Service examinations in India and Britain
  • Abolition of the Council of India in London
  • Reduction of taxation
  • Reduction of civil expenditure
  • Reduction of military expenditure
  • Greater Indian participation in administration
Importance
  • It had clearer nationalist objectives than the Madras Native Association.
  • It created political consensus across different parts of the Presidency.
  • It trained the first generation of nationalist leaders.
  • Several of its demands were later taken up by the Indian National Congress.
  • It helped connect regional politics with the emerging all-India movement.
Nationalist Press, Literature and Public Opinion

Newspapers, journals, poetry and political prose created a nationalist public sphere and carried anti-colonial ideas to English and Tamil readers.

The nationalist press created a public sphere in which colonial policies could be criticised and political ideas circulated.

Background

The appointment of T. Muthuswami Iyer as the first Indian judge of the Madras High Court produced strong opposition in the European-owned press.

Educated Indians recognised the need for newspapers that would express an Indian viewpoint.

The Hindu
  • The Hindu was founded in 1878.
  • G. Subramania Iyer and M. Veeraraghavachariar were among its principal founders.
  • They were joined by four associates.
  • The newspaper defended Indian interests.
  • It criticised racial discrimination and colonial administration.
  • It became an important vehicle of moderate nationalist opinion.
Swadesamitran
  • Swadesamitran was founded by G. Subramania Iyer.
  • The standard historical founding year is 1882.
  • It carried nationalist discussion to Tamil readers.
  • It helped expand political communication beyond the English-educated public.
  • Subramania Bharati was associated with the publication during part of his journalistic career.
Textual Caution

The 2019 English-medium SCERT textbook prints 1891 as the starting year of Swadesamitran. Standard newspaper histories generally use 1882. For factual notes, retain 1882 while recognising the textbook-printing discrepancy.

Subramania Bharati and Nationalist Journalism

Bharati communicated nationalism through:

  • Poetry
  • Political prose
  • Editorial writing
  • Translations
  • Public songs

Important journals associated with him include:

  • India
  • Vijaya
  • Swadesamitran

His writings promoted:

  • National independence
  • Swadeshi
  • Social equality
  • Women’s emancipation
  • Opposition to caste discrimination
  • National unity

Detailed literary treatment of Bharati belongs to Chapter 7.

Pondicherry Publications

French-controlled Pondicherry enabled nationalist literature to circulate outside direct British control.

Important publications included:

  • India
  • Vijaya
  • Suryodayam

British authorities treated several such writings as seditious and restricted their circulation.

Annie Besant’s Publications

Annie Besant used:

  • New India
  • Commonweal

These publications promoted Home Rule and constitutional self-government.

Role of the Press

The nationalist press:

  • Exposed colonial economic exploitation
  • Reported arrests and repression
  • Publicised political meetings
  • Popularised Swadeshi
  • Connected local struggles with all-India events
  • Created political awareness among Tamil readers
  • Enabled poets and journalists to become political mobilisers

The press did not merely report the freedom struggle; it became an instrument of the struggle.

Tamil Leaders and the Early Indian National Congress

Leaders from the Madras Presidency helped shape the early Congress through constitutional criticism, petitions, public meetings and legislative debate.

Political organisations in the Madras Presidency contributed to the formation and early development of the Indian National Congress.

Pre-Congress Meeting at Adyar

In December 1884, several political leaders met at the Theosophical Society.

Participants included:

  • Dadabhai Naoroji
  • K. T. Telang
  • Surendranath Banerjee
  • G. Subramania Iyer
  • P. Rangaiah Naidu
  • P. Anandacharlu

Such meetings helped create networks among leaders from different regions.

First Congress Session
  • Place — Bombay
  • Year — 1885
  • Total delegates — 72
  • Delegates from Madras — 22

The “Madras” figure refers to the larger Presidency, not only present-day Tamil Nadu.

Third Congress Session
  • Place — Madras
  • Year — 1887
  • Venue — Makkis Garden
  • Present association — Thousand Lights area
  • President — Badruddin Tyabji
  • Total delegates — 607
  • Delegates from the Madras Presidency — 362

Badruddin Tyabji was the first Muslim president of the Indian National Congress.

Important Moderate Leaders

Moderate leaders associated with the Madras Presidency included:

  • G. Subramania Iyer
  • P. Anandacharlu
  • S. Subramania Iyer
  • V. S. Srinivasa Sastri
  • P. S. Sivaswami Iyer
  • G. A. Natesan
  • V. Krishnaswami Iyer
Moderate Methods

The Moderates used:

  • Petitions
  • Resolutions
  • Memoranda
  • Public meetings
  • Legislative debate
  • Newspaper criticism
  • Evidence before official commissions
Contribution of the Moderates

They exposed:

  • Colonial economic exploitation
  • Racial inequality
  • The absence of representative government
  • The contradiction between British democracy at home and colonial rule in India

Their methods were constitutional, but their economic and political criticism helped build an intellectual foundation for later mass nationalism.

Swadeshi Movement and V. O. Chidambaranar

V.O.C. linked Swadeshi enterprise, labour mobilisation and political nationalism through the shipping company and the 1908 Thoothukudi–Tirunelveli movement.

The Partition of Bengal in 1905 stimulated the Swadeshi Movement throughout India.

In Tamil Nadu, the movement developed through:

  • Boycott of foreign goods
  • Promotion of indigenous industries
  • Public meetings
  • Political speeches in Tamil
  • Nationalist journalism
  • Student participation
  • Labour mobilisation

Thoothukudi became one of the major centres of Swadeshi activity in South India.

V. O. Chidambaranar

V. O. Chidambaram Pillai is popularly known as:

  • V.O.C.
  • Kappalottiya Tamizhan

He was:

  • A lawyer
  • A Swadeshi entrepreneur
  • A labour organiser
  • A political speaker
  • An associate of Subramania Siva and Bharati
Swadeshi Steam Navigation Company
  • The company was established in 1906.
  • Its centre was Thoothukudi.
  • It challenged the British India Steam Navigation Company.
  • Its service operated between Thoothukudi and Colombo.
  • V.O.C. acquired the ships Gallia and Lavo.
  • The venture represented economic resistance to British commercial monopoly.

The British administration assisted the European competitor and placed severe pressure on the Swadeshi company.

The company eventually failed commercially, but it became a powerful symbol of Swadeshi economic nationalism.

Coral Mills Strike
  • V.O.C. and Subramania Siva organised mill workers in Thoothukudi.
  • In 1908, workers of the European-owned Coral Mills went on strike.
  • Their demands included improved wages and working conditions.
  • The strike connected economic grievances with the nationalist movement.
Arrest of V.O.C. and Subramania Siva
  • Both leaders were arrested on charges of sedition.
  • V.O.C. initially received two life sentences.
  • News of their arrest triggered disturbances in Tirunelveli.
  • A police station, court building and municipal office were attacked or burned.
  • Police firing killed four people.
  • V.O.C. was subjected to severe prison labour, including pulling an oil press.
Importance

V.O.C.’s activities connected three major forms of resistance:

  • Swadeshi enterprise
  • Labour mobilisation
  • Political nationalism

V.O.C. must not be reduced only to the shipping company; his role in worker organisation and the Tirunelveli uprising is equally important.

Revolutionary Nationalism and Pondicherry

French Pondicherry became a centre for prohibited publications, revolutionary networks and the nationalist circle associated with Bharati, Aurobindo and V. V. S. Aiyar.

The suppression of the Swadeshi Movement pushed some young nationalists towards revolutionary methods.

Pondicherry as a Nationalist Centre

Pondicherry was under French rule and therefore outside the direct jurisdiction of British India.

It became a refuge for nationalists escaping British surveillance.

Important personalities associated with Pondicherry included:

  • Subramania Bharati
  • Aurobindo Ghosh
  • V. V. S. Aiyar
  • M. P. T. Acharya
  • T. S. S. Rajan

Pondicherry was used for:

  • Publishing nationalist literature
  • Distributing prohibited publications
  • Political discussion
  • Contact with revolutionary networks
  • Training and ideological exchange
Bharata Mata Society
  • Nilakanta Brahmachari and his associates organised the Bharata Mata Society.
  • It functioned as a secret revolutionary organisation.
  • It promoted militant opposition to British rule.
  • Vanchinathan was influenced by this revolutionary network.
Vanchinathan and the Ashe Assassination
  • Vanchinathan belonged to Senkottai.
  • Date — 17 June 1911
  • Place — Maniyachi railway junction
  • Target — Robert William d’Escourt Ashe
  • Ashe was the Collector of Tirunelveli.
  • Vanchinathan shot Ashe inside a railway carriage.
  • Vanchinathan then shot himself.

Maniyachi later became closely associated with Vanchinathan’s memory.

Difference from V.O.C.’s Method

V.O.C. used:

  • Swadeshi enterprise
  • Labour organisation
  • Public mobilisation

Vanchinathan used:

  • Individual revolutionary violence
  • Secret organisational networks

Both opposed colonial rule, but their methods were fundamentally different.

Revolutionary nationalism inspired sacrifice but did not develop the same mass base as the later Gandhian movements.

Home Rule Movement and Annie Besant

Annie Besant’s Home Rule League used newspapers, lectures, classes and student volunteers to demand self-government during the First World War.

The Home Rule Movement revived organised nationalism during the First World War.

Annie Besant

Annie Besant was:

  • An Irish political activist
  • A leader of the Theosophical Society
  • Associated with Adyar in Madras
  • A journalist
  • A campaigner for Indian self-government
Home Rule League
  • Annie Besant started her Home Rule League in 1916.
  • It was influenced by the Irish Home Rule movement.
  • It demanded self-government for India.
  • It initially accepted nominal allegiance to the British Crown.

Important associates included:

  • G. S. Arundale
  • B. P. Wadia
  • C. P. Ramaswami Aiyar
Methods

The movement used:

  • Newspapers
  • Political pamphlets
  • Public speeches
  • Lectures
  • Home Rule classes
  • Branch organisations
  • Student volunteers
  • Political tours
Newspapers

Annie Besant promoted Home Rule through:

  • New India
  • Commonweal
Student Participation
  • Students joined Home Rule classes.
  • Volunteer groups and scout-like formations were organised.
  • The movement drew young people into politics.
  • The government attempted to restrict student participation.
Government Repression
  • Annie Besant and her associates were interned.
  • They were restricted from public speaking and political activity.
  • Their internment produced widespread protest.
  • The agitation increased the popularity of Home Rule.
Congress Presidency

Annie Besant became president of the Indian National Congress in 1917.

B. P. Wadia

B. P. Wadia linked:

  • Home Rule politics
  • Labour organisation
  • Trade-union activity

The movement declined after Gandhi emerged as the principal leader of mass nationalism, but it prepared students, workers and middle-class activists for later campaigns.

Rowlatt, Khilafat and Non-Cooperation Movements

Rowlatt protest, Khilafat and Non-Cooperation expanded nationalism through hartals, boycott, khadi, temperance, workers and Hindu–Muslim cooperation.

Rowlatt Act

The Rowlatt Act was passed in 1919.

It permitted:

  • Detention without ordinary judicial safeguards
  • Imprisonment of persons suspected of revolutionary activity
  • Extraordinary restrictions on civil liberties

It became popularly known as the Black Act.

Rowlatt Satyagraha in Madras
  • Gandhi addressed a meeting at Marina Beach on 18 March 1919.
  • A hartal was observed on 6 April 1919.
  • Processions from different parts of Madras converged at Marina Beach.
  • Participants observed fasting and prayer.
  • The Madras Satyagraha Sabha was formed.

Important participants included:

  • C. Rajagopalachari
  • S. Satyamurti
  • Kasturiranga Iyengar
  • George Joseph

A separate workers’ meeting was addressed by:

  • Thiru. Vi. Kalyanasundaram
  • B. P. Wadia
  • V. O. Chidambaranar

Workers, students and women participated in large numbers.

Khilafat Movement

The Khilafat Movement emerged after the First World War in defence of the Ottoman Caliph.

Important Tamil Nadu facts:

  • Khilafat Day was observed on 17 April 1920.
  • Maulana Shaukat Ali presided over an important meeting.
  • A Khilafat conference was held at Erode.
  • Vaniyambadi became a major centre of Khilafat activity.

The movement temporarily strengthened Hindu–Muslim cooperation within the national struggle.

Non-Cooperation Movement

Important leaders in Tamil Nadu included:

  • C. Rajagopalachari
  • E. V. Ramasamy
  • Yakub Hasan

Rajaji worked closely with Yakub Hasan of the Muslim League.

Main Activities
  • Boycott of legislative councils
  • Boycott of government schools
  • Boycott of law courts
  • Boycott of foreign goods
  • Promotion of khadi
  • Liquor-shop picketing
  • Hartals
  • Worker strikes
  • Volunteer organisations
  • No-tax campaigns
  • Opposition to the Criminal Tribes Act
  • Boycott of the Prince of Wales’s visit

A no-tax campaign took place in Thanjavur.

E. V. Ramasamy’s Congress Phase

During this phase, E. V. Ramasamy:

  • Promoted khadi
  • Participated in temperance campaigns
  • Supported liquor-shop picketing
  • Participated in the Vaikom Satyagraha
  • Faced imprisonment

His later rationalist, Self-Respect and Dravidian activities belong to Chapters 23–28 and should not be repeated here.

Withdrawal

The Non-Cooperation Movement was withdrawn in 1922 after the Chauri Chaura incident.

Civil Disobedience and Vedaranyam Salt Satyagraha

Rajaji’s Vedaranyam march became Tamil Nadu’s major Salt Satyagraha, while wider Civil Disobedience included coastal protests, flag actions and mass arrests.

The Civil Disobedience Movement began nationally with Gandhi’s Dandi Salt March in 1930.

In Tamil Nadu, Rajaji organised a parallel march to Vedaranyam.

Vedaranyam Salt March
  • Leader — C. Rajagopalachari
  • Starting place — Tiruchirappalli
  • Starting date — 13 April 1930
  • Destination — Vedaranyam
  • Arrival date — 28 April 1930
  • Coastal salt-law action — Vedaranyam region

Twelve volunteers under Rajaji’s leadership broke the salt law by collecting salt.

Rajaji was arrested.

Important Participants
  • T. S. S. Rajan
  • Rukmini Lakshmipathi
  • Sardar A. Vedarathnam
  • C. Swaminatha Chettiar
  • K. Santhanam

Namakkal V. Ramalingam Pillai composed a special marching song for the volunteers.

Wider Agitations

Civil Disobedience was not confined to Vedaranyam.

Salt-law protests and related actions occurred at:

  • Madras
  • Rameswaram
  • Uvari
  • Veppalodai
  • Thoothukudi
  • Tharuvaikulam

T. Prakasam and K. Nageswara Rao established a satyagraha camp at Udayavanam near Madras.

Other activities included:

  • Picketing shops selling foreign goods
  • Boycott of foreign cloth
  • Hartals
  • Worker strikes
  • Public processions
  • Patriotic songs
  • Swadeshi dramas
Rukmini Lakshmipathi

Rukmini Lakshmipathi participated in the Vedaranyam march and became an important woman participant in the Salt Satyagraha.

Her full contribution belongs to Chapter 19.

Bhashyam, Also Known as Arya
  • Bhashyam was popularly known as Arya.
  • He hoisted the national flag at Fort St. George.
  • Date — 26 January 1932.
Tiruppur Kumaran
  • Original name — O. K. S. R. Kumarasamy
  • A nationalist procession was held at Tiruppur on 11 January 1932.
  • Police attacked the procession.
  • Kumaran died while holding the national flag.
  • He became known as Kodikatha Kumaran.
Essential Distinction
  • Dandi March — led by Gandhi in Gujarat
  • Vedaranyam March — led by Rajaji in Tamil Nadu

Tiruppur Kumaran participated in the wider Civil Disobedience environment; he was not a marcher in the Vedaranyam expedition.

Labour, Students and Mass Mobilisation

Workers, students and constructive programmes transformed nationalism from an educated elite movement into broad social mobilisation.

Tamil Nadu’s freedom struggle gradually expanded from educated political associations into a broad mass movement.

Labour Participation
Coral Mills
  • Coral Mills workers went on strike at Thoothukudi in 1908.
  • V.O.C. and Subramania Siva supported their demands.
  • The strike linked labour issues with Swadeshi nationalism.
Madras Labour Union
  • The Madras Labour Union was formed in 1918.
  • It was among the earliest organised trade unions in India.
  • B. P. Wadia was an important organiser.
  • Thiru. Vi. Ka. and other public figures supported labour organisation.
Madurai Labour Union
  • George Joseph helped workers of Harvey Mills establish the Madurai Labour Union in 1918.
  • Early struggles secured higher wages and reduced working hours.
Workers in National Movements

Workers participated in:

  • Rowlatt Satyagraha
  • Non-Cooperation
  • Civil Disobedience
  • Quit India

Important striking groups during Quit India included:

  • Buckingham and Carnatic Mills workers
  • Madras Port Trust workers
  • Madras Corporation workers
  • Electric Tramway workers
Student Participation

Students participated in:

  • Swadeshi meetings
  • Home Rule classes
  • Volunteer organisations
  • Rowlatt protests
  • Simon Commission boycott
  • Civil Disobedience
  • Quit India

Students helped by:

  • Distributing pamphlets
  • Carrying flags
  • Organising processions
  • Boycotting classes
  • Attending political lectures
  • Spreading nationalist messages
Constructive Programme

Nationalist mass mobilisation included:

  • Khadi production
  • Spinning
  • Foreign-cloth boycott
  • Temperance
  • Liquor-shop picketing
  • National education
  • Removal of untouchability
  • Village work
  • Hindu–Muslim cooperation
Importance

Labour and student participation transformed nationalism from an elite political activity into a broader social movement.

Detailed independent labour history and later socio-political movements belong to Chapters 20 and 21.

Swarajists and Major Congress Leaders

Swarajists used legislative obstruction, while Rajaji, Satyamurti and Kamaraj represented different strategies within Congress politics and mass struggle.

Pro-Changers and No-Changers

After the withdrawal of the Non-Cooperation Movement, Congress leaders disagreed about participation in legislative councils.

No-Changers

They wanted to:

  • Continue the boycott of councils
  • Promote khadi
  • Carry out constructive work
  • Prepare people for future mass action

Rajaji was an important No-Changer in the Madras Presidency.

Pro-Changers or Swarajists

They wanted to:

  • Contest council elections
  • Enter the legislatures
  • Expose colonial administration from within
  • Obstruct unjust government measures

The Swaraj Party was founded nationally by:

  • C. R. Das
  • Motilal Nehru

Tamil Swarajist leaders included:

  • S. Srinivasa Iyengar
  • S. Satyamurti
Neill Statue Agitation

A statue of Colonel James Neill stood on Mount Road in Madras.

Nationalists opposed the statue because Neill was associated with brutal repression during the Revolt of 1857.

Important facts:

  • The agitation took place in 1927.
  • S. N. Somayajulu of Tirunelveli led the protests.
  • Protesters came from different parts of the Presidency.
  • Several participants were arrested.
  • Gandhi supported the agitation.
  • The statue was moved to the Madras Museum after the Congress ministry came to power in 1937.
Simon Commission Boycott

The Simon Commission contained no Indian member.

Tamil Nadu facts:

  • S. Satyamurti headed the Simon Boycott Propaganda Committee in Madras.
  • The Commission arrived in Madras on 18 February 1929.
  • Hartals and demonstrations were organised.
  • Black flags were shown.
  • Students, lawyers, traders and commuters participated.
  • The police used force to suppress protests.
Madras Congress Session of 1927
  • The Indian National Congress met at Madras in 1927.
  • The session adopted complete independence as an objective.
  • It also called for opposition to the Simon Commission.
  • This preceded the formal adoption of Poorna Swaraj at Lahore in 1929.
Rajaji

Freedom-struggle associations include:

  • Rowlatt Satyagraha
  • Non-Cooperation
  • Constructive work
  • No-Changer position
  • Vedaranyam Salt Satyagraha
  • Congress organisation
  • First Congress ministry in the Madras Presidency

In 1937, Rajaji formed the first Congress ministry under provincial autonomy.

The Congress ministries resigned in 1939 after Britain involved India in the Second World War without consulting elected Indian representatives.

S. Satyamurti

Important associations:

  • Swaraj Party
  • Legislative politics
  • Simon Commission boycott
  • Civil liberties
  • Congress organisation
  • Foreign-cloth boycott
  • Public speeches and political education
K. Kamaraj

Freedom-struggle associations include:

  • Grassroots Congress organisation
  • Civil Disobedience
  • Imprisonment
  • Congress organisational work
  • Quit India mobilisation

His post-Independence career must not be added to this chapter.

Quit India Movement and INA Participation

Quit India in Tamil Nadu was decentralised and militant, while Tamil communities in Southeast Asia supported the INA and the Rani of Jhansi Regiment.

Background

The immediate background included:

  • Failure of the Cripps Mission
  • Wartime shortages
  • Price rise
  • Britain’s refusal to transfer power immediately
  • Growing public anger against colonial rule

The Quit India resolution was passed on 8 August 1942.

Gandhi gave the call:

  • Do or Die

The British arrested most senior Congress leaders immediately.

Kamaraj’s Role
  • Kamaraj was returning from Bombay after the adoption of the movement.
  • Police waited at railway stations to arrest local leaders.
  • He got down at Arakkonam.
  • He travelled secretly and worked underground.
  • He helped communicate the movement’s instructions and organise resistance.
  • He was later imprisoned for his participation.
Forms of Protest in Tamil Nadu

Activities included:

  • Worker strikes
  • Student demonstrations
  • Burning of post offices and public buildings
  • Cutting telegraph and telephone lines
  • Disruption of railway traffic
  • Attacks on symbols of colonial authority
  • Distribution of underground pamphlets
Major Centres and Incidents
  • Buckingham and Carnatic Mills workers struck work.
  • Madras Port Trust workers participated.
  • Madras Corporation workers participated.
  • Electric Tramway workers joined.
  • Public buildings were attacked at Vellore and Panapakkam.
  • Sulur airport was attacked.
  • Trains were derailed near Coimbatore.
  • Congress volunteers clashed with military forces in Madurai.
  • Police firing occurred at Rajapalayam, Karaikudi and Devakottai.
  • College students took part in protests.

The movement became decentralised because the recognised leadership had been arrested.

Rajaji and Quit India: Historical Caution

Rajaji differed from Gandhi and the Congress leadership over the Quit India resolution and did not join the movement.

Some editions of the Tamil Nadu school textbook contain a conflicting sentence placing Rajaji in the distribution of Quit India pamphlets. Standard biographical accounts state that he opposed and remained outside the movement.

Do not present Rajaji as a principal organiser of Quit India.

Indian National Army

The Indian National Army was initially organised under Mohan Singh from Indian prisoners of war and expatriate communities in Southeast Asia.

Subhas Chandra Bose later reorganised it.

Important associations:

  • Azad Hind Fauj
  • Provisional Government of Free India
  • Gandhi Brigade
  • Nehru Brigade
  • Rani of Jhansi Regiment
Tamil Participation
  • Tamil communities in Malaya and Singapore supplied volunteers and material support.
  • Young Tamil men and women joined the INA.
  • Tamil diaspora networks helped raise funds and organise recruitment.
Captain Lakshmi Sahgal
  • Captain Lakshmi Sahgal led the Rani of Jhansi Regiment.
  • It was the women’s regiment of the INA.
  • She was also associated with the Provisional Government of Azad Hind.

Her complete biography and the wider contribution of women belong to Chapter 19.

Importance

Tamil Nadu’s final phase of anti-colonial participation combined:

  • Underground Congress activity within the Presidency
  • Worker and student resistance
  • Armed nationalist mobilisation among the Tamil diaspora

The Quit India Movement in Tamil Nadu was suppressed with severe force, but anti-colonial resistance continued until independence.

Rapid Revision and High-Yield Distinctions

The final topic consolidates chronology, leader–place, organisation and publication associations, movement distinctions and common examination traps.

High-Yield Distinctions
Madras Presidency versus Present-Day Tamil Nadu

Madras Presidency

  • Larger British province
  • Included territories outside modern Tamil Nadu

Present-day Tamil Nadu

  • Smaller present political boundary
  • Presidency statistics cannot automatically be treated as Tamil Nadu-only figures
Early Resistance versus Organised Nationalism

Early resistance

  • Regional rulers and Palayakkarars
  • Armed conflict
  • Defence of local sovereignty
  • Eighteenth and early nineteenth centuries

Organised nationalism

  • Associations, newspapers and Congress
  • Province-wide and all-India networks
  • Constitutional and mass methods
  • Mainly from the later nineteenth century
Madras Native Association versus Madras Mahajana Sabha

Madras Native Association

  • 1852
  • Mainly merchants
  • Taxation and public grievances
  • Ceased by 1862

Madras Mahajana Sabha

  • 1884
  • Clear nationalist objectives
  • Training ground for Congress leaders
  • Simultaneous Civil Service examinations and administrative reforms
The Hindu versus Swadesamitran

The Hindu

  • English
  • Founded in 1878

Swadesamitran

  • Tamil
  • Standard founding year 1882
  • Took nationalist ideas to Tamil readers
V.O.C. versus Vanchinathan

V.O.C.

  • Swadeshi enterprise
  • Labour organisation
  • Public political mobilisation

Vanchinathan

  • Secret revolutionary network
  • Assassination of Ashe
Bharati versus Subramania Siva

Bharati

  • Poetry
  • Prose
  • Journalism
  • Nationalist ideas

Subramania Siva

  • Public speaking
  • Touring
  • Direct mobilisation
  • Repeated imprisonment
Home Rule versus Non-Cooperation

Home Rule

  • Constitutional self-government
  • Annie Besant
  • Press, lectures and political classes

Non-Cooperation

  • Boycott of colonial institutions
  • Gandhi, Rajaji and E. V. Ramasamy
  • Khadi, temperance and mass mobilisation
Rowlatt Satyagraha versus Civil Disobedience

Rowlatt Satyagraha

  • 1919
  • Protest against detention powers
  • Hartal, fasting and prayer

Civil Disobedience

  • 1930 onward
  • Open violation of colonial laws
  • Salt Satyagraha and foreign-goods boycott
Dandi March versus Vedaranyam March

Dandi

  • Gujarat
  • Led by Gandhi

Vedaranyam

  • Tamil Nadu
  • Led by Rajaji
Rajaji versus Kamaraj in 1942

Rajaji

  • Opposed the Quit India resolution
  • Did not organise the movement

Kamaraj

  • Worked underground
  • Organised people
  • Was imprisoned for participation
Tamil Nadu Movement versus INA Participation

Within Tamil Nadu

  • Congress mobilisation
  • Worker strikes
  • Student protests
  • Underground activity

INA participation

  • Centred largely in Southeast Asia
  • Supported by Indian and Tamil diaspora communities
  • Included the Rani of Jhansi Regiment
Exam Traps
  • Madras Presidency was not identical to present-day Tamil Nadu.
  • V.O.C. founded a Swadeshi shipping company; he was not a revolutionary assassin.
  • Vanchinathan assassinated Ashe at Maniyachi in 1911.
  • Gandhi led the Dandi March; Rajaji led the Vedaranyam March.
  • Tiruppur Kumaran died during wider Civil Disobedience activity, not during the Vedaranyam march.
  • The Madras Native Association was founded in 1852; the Madras Mahajana Sabha in 1884.
  • The Hindu was founded in 1878.
  • Use 1882 as the standard founding year of Swadesamitran, while recognising the conflicting year in one SCERT English edition.
  • Annie Besant started her Home Rule League in 1916 and became Congress president in 1917.
  • S. Satyamurti was a Swarajist; Rajaji was initially a No-Changer.
  • Rajaji opposed Quit India; Kamaraj actively organised it.
  • Captain Lakshmi Sahgal is associated with the Rani of Jhansi Regiment.
  • Detailed early rebellions belong to Chapter 18.
  • Detailed women freedom fighters belong to Chapter 19.
